content: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, paralytic, and inflammatory disorder affecting the peripheral nervous system. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) has been shown to be beneficial in treating other autoimmune diseases. This review is an updated analysis of IVIg for GBS, building on previous reviews published between 2001 and 2012. Other systematic reviews have demonstrated that plasma exchange (PE) significantly accelerates recovery in GBS compared to supportive care alone, while corticosteroids alone are ineffective. The objectives of this review were fourfold: (1) to evaluate the efficacy of IVIg in accelerating recovery and reducing long-term disability in GBS; (2) to determine the optimal dose of IVIg for these outcomes; (3) to compare the efficacy of IVIg with PE or immunoabsorption; and (4) to assess whether combining IVIg with PE offers additional benefits compared to PE alone. The search strategy included databases such as the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to December 2013. Bibliographies of randomized trials were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to identify additional data. The inclusion criteria were randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing IVIg with no treatment, placebo, PE, or other immunomodulatory therapies in children and adults with GBS of varying severity. Trials combining IVIg with other treatments were also included. Two independent reviewers selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the evidence. Adverse events reported in the trials were also analyzed. A total of 12 trials met the inclusion criteria. Seven trials, involving 623 severely affected participants, compared IVIg with PE. In five trials with 536 participants, the mean difference in improvement on a seven-grade disability scale after four weeks was minimal and not statistically significant between IVIg and PE (mean difference [MD] 0.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.20 to 0.25). Other outcome measures also showed no significant differences between the two treatments. Three studies involving 75 children suggested that IVIg significantly accelerates recovery compared to supportive care. In one trial with 21 mildly affected children, IVIg led to significantly greater improvement in disability grade after four weeks compared to supportive care alone (MD 1.42, 95% CI 0.27 to 2.57). In a trial of 249 participants comparing PE followed by IVIg with PE alone, the combined treatment group showed a mean improvement of 0.2 grades (95% CI -0.14 to 0.54) over PE alone, which was not clinically significant but did not rule out the possibility of additional benefit. Another trial with 34 participants comparing immunoabsorption followed by IVIg with immunoabsorption alone found no significant additional benefit from the combined treatment. Adverse events were not significantly more frequent with IVIg compared to PE. However, IVIg was significantly more likely to be completed than PE. In one trial involving 51 children, there was no significant difference in outcomes when the standard dose of IVIg was administered over two days versus five days. The authors concluded that previous evidence supports the use of PE to accelerate recovery compared to supportive care alone. While there are no adequate comparisons of IVIg with placebo in adults, moderate-quality evidence suggests that IVIg, when initiated within two weeks of symptom onset, is as effective as PE in severe cases of GBS. Adverse events were comparable between IVIg and PE, but IVIg was more likely to be completed. Moderate-quality evidence also indicates that adding IVIg after PE does not provide significant additional benefit. In children, low-quality evidence suggests that IVIg likely accelerates recovery compared to supportive care alone. Further research is needed to evaluate IVIg in mild cases of GBS, in patients treated more than two weeks after symptom onset, and to determine the optimal dosing regimen. A dose-ranging study is currently underway.
